Summary

This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting a pretrained autoregressive text LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and latency-tolerant interaction. The key ideas are: (1) injecting coarse timing via periodic synchronization/speaker tokens into interleaved dual-speaker speech-token sequences; (2) training on deduplicated HuBERT tokens to improve semantic density while preserving timing through periodic tags; (3) predicting short future chunks for both speakers to tolerate one-chunk latency (160–240 ms); and (4) a three-stage training recipe that relies heavily on synthetic spoken dialogue generated from text dialogue corpora, followed by fine-tuning on about 2k hours of real dual-channel spoken dialogue. The paper reports improved semantic quality over dGSLM, comparable naturalness, some OOD robustness, and simulated interaction results between two SyncLLM agents.

Overall assessment

This is an interesting and timely paper on an important problem: moving beyond turn-based spoken interfaces toward genuinely synchronous dialogue. The paper’s central framing is compelling, and the proposed sequence formatting plus latency-aware generation mechanism are novel enough to be of broad interest. The empirical results suggest a meaningful semantic advantage over dGSLM while preserving turn-taking naturalness, which is a strong outcome if it holds under careful scrutiny.

That said, I have substantial concerns about evaluation methodology, fairness of comparisons, and clarity around what exactly is being measured. The paper’s strongest claims are about “full-duplex dialogue agents” and “latency-tolerant interaction,” but much of the evidence comes from continuation-mode generation and simulated model-model interaction rather than real interactive human-agent experiments. In addition, the semantic evaluation via ASR transcription and text-model perplexity is indirect and potentially confounded. The human evaluation is promising, but the design and statistical reporting leave open questions. I therefore view the paper as strong in idea and engineering, but somewhat weaker in validation.

Strengths

1. Important problem and strong motivation
The paper addresses a real limitation of current spoken dialogue systems: most are effectively half-duplex and turn-based. The motivation from human conversational dynamics is well articulated and convincing.

2. Clever sequence design
The use of periodic synchronization tokens to impose coarse wall-clock structure on an autoregressive LLM is elegant. The deduplication/interpolation scheme is also practically motivated and easy to understand.

3. Latency-aware formulation
The explicit treatment of delayed user input and one-chunk-ahead estimation is a meaningful systems contribution. This is more realistic than assuming immediate access to the interlocutor stream.

4. Practical training recipe
The three-stage pipeline leveraging large-scale synthetic spoken dialogue is sensible and likely useful beyond this paper. The ability to get reasonable behavior from only ~2k hours of real spoken dialogue is notable.

5. Broad empirical scope
The paper includes automatic semantic evaluation, turn-taking correlation metrics, human judgments, OOD testing, and simulated interaction. Even if some evaluations are imperfect, the breadth is appreciated.

Main weaknesses

1. The evidence for “full-duplex interaction” is still indirect
The paper’s headline claim is about full-duplex dialogue agents, but the main evaluations are continuation generation and simulated LLM-LLM interaction. There is no real-time human-agent study showing that users can interrupt, overlap, backchannel, or recover from latency in practice. This weakens the practical significance of the claims.

2. Baseline comparison may not be fully fair
dGSLM is the main baseline, but it differs from SyncLLM in many dimensions beyond synchrony modeling: architecture, pretraining regime, access to text knowledge, synthetic data scale, and likely tokenizer/vocoder choices. The paper argues this is a feature, but then the comparison does not isolate which component drives gains. The semantic gains may largely come from inheriting Llama3’s text knowledge rather than from the synchronous formulation itself.

3. Semantic evaluation is indirect and somewhat fragile
Using ASR transcripts of generated speech, collapsing overlaps into turn-based text, and then scoring with a text dialogue model’s perplexity is several steps removed from the actual task. This may systematically favor models whose outputs are easier for ASR or more text-like, rather than better spoken dialogue models. It also discards overlap information, which is central to the paper.

4. Naturalness metric is limited
The turn-taking evaluation uses correlation of average event durations with ground truth continuations given the same prompt. This is a weak proxy for naturalness. Correlation of averages can hide substantial distributional mismatch and does not directly assess whether generated overlaps/backchannels occur in appropriate places.

5. Human evaluation needs more detail and stronger analysis
The MOS study is useful, but only 3 raters per item is fairly light, and the paper does not report inter-rater agreement, significance testing between key systems, or enough detail on prompt balancing and randomization. Also, “meaningfulness” and “naturalness” are broad constructs; more targeted pairwise preference studies might have been more informative.

6. Missing or unclear ablations
The paper introduces several components: periodic sync tokens, deduplication, interpolation, future user-chunk estimation, synthetic stage 1, synthetic stage 2, and real stage 3. There is little ablation isolating their contributions. This makes it hard to know what is essential.

Detailed comments

On novelty

The paper’s novelty lies less in a new model architecture and more in a representation/training/inference framework for synchronous spoken dialogue with standard autoregressive LLMs. I think this is a legitimate and interesting contribution. The periodic synchronization token idea is simple but effective. The latency-tolerant “predict the missing current user chunk, then generate next self chunk” mechanism is also a nice insight.

However, the paper should be more precise in distinguishing:
- full-duplex continuation modeling,
- simulated duplex interaction under one-chunk delay,
- actual deployed interactive spoken dialogue.

Currently these are sometimes conflated.

On technical clarity

The paper is mostly understandable, but several aspects need clarification:

1. Chunk generation order and causality
The model predicts “its side” followed by “user side” in each chunk during training. At inference for interaction, it predicts an estimated user chunk and then its next chunk. I had to read this multiple times to understand the exact ordering. A more formal algorithm or pseudocode would help.

2. Why [S0] must always be present but [S1] may be omitted
This is explained, but the asymmetry raises questions. Does this bias the model toward one speaker role? Was role randomization used during training?

3. Interpolation heuristic
Repeating deduplicated tokens equally within a chunk seems crude. The paper says the effect is imperceptible, but no objective or subjective evidence is shown. Since speech quality and timing are central, this deserves more support.

4. Synthetic data generation
The paper says 212k hours of synthetic spoken dialogue are generated from text dialogue data, but details are sparse. What datasets exactly? What filtering? How diverse are speakers/prosody if Bark with 10 presets is used? Could synthetic artifacts leak into evaluation behavior?

5. Computational cost
Training Llama3-8B over these stages with 212k hours equivalent data is nontrivial. The paper should report training compute, sequence lengths, and inference latency.

On evaluation

Semantic evaluation:
- The ASR-perplexity metric is creative but problematic.
- It depends on ASR quality, which may vary by model and speech naturalness.
- It ignores overlap by converting to turn-based text.
- It uses a text dialogue model as judge, which may reward generic text coherence rather than spoken conversational appropriateness.

I would strongly prefer additional semantic metrics:
- human pairwise preference on relevance/coherence,
- transcript-based response appropriateness judged by annotators,
- perhaps LLM-as-judge with careful controls,
- or task-based evaluations if applicable.

Naturalness evaluation:
The turn-taking event correlation metric comes from prior work, but the paper should acknowledge its limitations more explicitly. Correlation with ground-truth continuation durations given the same prompt does not necessarily mean the generated dialogue is natural; many plausible continuations could differ from the reference. This is especially true for open-ended dialogue.

Human evaluation:
The MOS results are encouraging, especially the large gap in meaningfulness over dGSLM. But some issues remain:
- Why is dGSLM so low on meaningfulness (1.55) while naturalness is near 4? This suggests either a severe semantic failure or a mismatch in evaluation setup.
- The paper should report significance tests for SyncLLM-F vs SyncLLM-C vs Re-synth, not just confidence intervals.
- It would help to know whether raters heard stereo/channel-separated audio or mixed audio, since overlap perception depends on presentation.
- Since the task is about full-duplex interaction, raters should ideally evaluate interruption handling, backchannel appropriateness, and responsiveness separately.

Interaction evaluation:
The simulated LLM-LLM interaction is interesting, but it is not a substitute for human interaction. Also, if both sides are generated by similar models, coherence may be artificially easier than with real users. The F-C experiment helps somewhat, but still remains model-model.

Missing baselines and ablations

The paper would be much stronger with the following:

1. Ablation on synchronization tokens
What happens without periodic sync tokens, or with absolute time embeddings, or with chunk-index embeddings?

2. Ablation on deduplication
How much does deduplication help semantics and hurt/help timing?

3. Ablation on future user-chunk estimation
Compare interaction quality with and without estimated user chunk, and under varying latency.

4. Ablation on training stages
How much does each stage contribute? In particular, does stage 2 materially help beyond stage 1 + stage 3?

5. Comparison to simpler cascaded systems
A strong ASR-LLM-TTS streaming baseline with turn-taking heuristics would be useful. The paper argues against half-duplex systems conceptually, but practical baselines matter.

6. Comparison to text-conditioned spoken dialogue models
Since much of the gain may come from text pretraining, compare against a turn-based speech/text LLM adapted with a simpler duplex wrapper.

Questions for the authors

1. How often does the estimated user chunk differ substantially from the true user chunk, and how sensitive is downstream generation to this mismatch?
2. Did you randomize speaker-role assignment during training so that either side could be “the model”?
3. What is the actual end-to-end latency budget including tokenization, model inference, interpolation, and vocoding?
4. How robust is the method to ASR/tokenization errors from real microphone input, noise, accents, or non-telephone speech?
5. How often does the model produce pathological overlap, e.g., speaking over the user too aggressively?
6. Can the model intentionally choose to remain silent/backchannel, or is it biased to fill every chunk with output?
7. Why were chunk sizes limited to 160/200/240 ms? What happens below 160 ms or above 240 ms?
8. How much of the semantic gain remains if dGSLM is given stronger text-informed pretraining or synthetic data?

Minor comments

1. There are several grammatical issues and typos throughout the paper.
Examples include:
- “so that they run synchronously” should be “so that it runs synchronously” or “the models run synchronously”
- “for help our model learn” should be “to help our model learn”
- “is are almost the same” should be corrected
A careful proofreading is needed.

2. Figure 7 appears missing in the provided text (“NOT_FOUND”). This is problematic if the figure is important to the interaction claims.

3. The notation around speaker tags and chunk formatting could be made more formal.

4. The paper should define exactly how prompts are selected and whether prompt lengths are matched across datasets.

5. The use of “Internet-scale latencies” up to 240 ms is plausible, but many real systems experience larger tail latencies. The claim should be softened or expanded with broader latency analysis.

Recommendation

Weak Accept

Rationale

I think the paper presents a genuinely interesting direction with a simple, elegant core idea and promising results. The notion of synchronizing an autoregressive LLM to wall-clock time via periodic tokens, combined with latency-aware chunk prediction, is novel and likely to inspire follow-up work. The practical training recipe using synthetic spoken dialogue is also valuable.

However, I am not fully convinced by the current evaluation as evidence for the strongest claims. The comparisons do not cleanly isolate the contribution of synchrony modeling versus text-pretrained semantics, and the interaction results remain simulated rather than real. With stronger ablations and more direct interactive evaluation, this could become a very strong paper.

Confidence

3/5

I am reasonably confident in my assessment of the paper’s strengths and weaknesses, though some concerns could be resolved by details likely present in appendices or supplementary material not included here.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting an autoregressive LLM (Llama3-8B) into a full-duplex spoken dialogue agent that can model overlapping speech, backchannels, and latency-tolerant interaction. The core idea is to inject wall-clock synchrony via periodic speaker synchronization tokens and to train on interleaved, deduplicated HuBERT token chunks from both speakers. To address limited real spoken-dialogue data, the authors use a three-stage training recipe with large-scale synthetic speech generated from text dialogue data, followed by finetuning on about 2k hours of real dual-channel dialogue. Experiments compare against dGSLM and report substantially better semantic quality, comparable or slightly better turn-taking naturalness, some out-of-distribution robustness, and plausible interaction under simulated one-chunk latency.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving beyond turn-based spoken interfaces toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex dialogue.
Technically novel framing of synchrony through periodic speaker/time tokens and chunked interleaving of two dialogue streams within a standard autoregressive LLM.
Practical latency-aware design: predicting the user's current chunk to generate the agent's next chunk is a reasonable mechanism for coping with real-time delays.
Strong use of pretrained text LLM knowledge, combined with synthetic speech data, to overcome scarcity of real spoken-dialogue corpora.
Three-stage training recipe is intuitive and well motivated, progressively bridging text dialogue, synthetic duplex formatting, and real spoken turn-taking cues.
Empirical results suggest clear gains in semantic meaningfulness over the main baseline, including on out-of-distribution evaluation.
Human evaluation includes both meaningfulness and naturalness, which is appropriate for spoken dialogue generation.
The paper is generally well motivated and clearly explains the representation choices, especially deduplication and interpolation.
weaknesses: The main baseline comparison is narrow; dGSLM is relevant, but stronger contemporary speech-text or speech-native dialogue baselines are not extensively compared.
Evaluation of semantics relies heavily on ASR transcription and text-model perplexity, which may imperfectly reflect spoken-dialogue quality and may discard overlap information.
The human study is relatively small (32 annotators, 180 items, 3 ratings/item), making fine-grained claims such as parity in naturalness somewhat tentative.
The reported naturalness gains over dGSLM are modest or mixed; the strongest improvements are in meaningfulness rather than full-duplex conversational realism.
The interpolation heuristic for reconstructing deduplicated tokens may distort timing/prosody, but its impact is not rigorously quantified beyond anecdotal observation.
The interaction setting is simulated via model-model interaction with one-chunk latency rather than real user interaction, so claims about practical deployment remain somewhat indirect.
The paper does not deeply analyze failure modes such as interruption handling errors, hallucinated backchannels, or instability over long conversations.

Some implementation and training details that would matter for reproducibility and interpretation appear limited in the provided text, such as optimization specifics and statistical significance testing for several comparisons.
soundness_issues: The core methodology is plausible and mostly sound, but several claims are supported by proxy metrics rather than direct task-grounded evaluation of full-duplex interaction quality.
Semantic evaluation converts generated speech to text and ignores overlapping speech, which may systematically under-measure or mis-measure the very synchronous phenomena the paper targets.

Turn-taking naturalness is evaluated via correlation of event durations with ground-truth continuations given the same prompt; this is informative but not a definitive measure of conversational appropriateness or causal turn-taking skill.

The latency-tolerance claim is demonstrated in simulation up to chunk sizes of 240 ms, but there is no real networked end-to-end deployment evidence, so robustness to practical systems issues remains only partially validated.

Synthetic data generation via Bark TTS may imprint artifacts or unnatural timing patterns; the paper motivates this strategy well, but does not fully disentangle how much performance comes from synthetic-data scale versus architectural choices.

The deduplication/interpolation design introduces an approximation to duration modeling; while likely workable, the paper does not provide ablations isolating the effect of this approximation on semantic fidelity and timing naturalness.
